name: Ractopamine (Paylean)

lead: Ractopamine is a livestock feed additive that promotes lean muscle, and it appears in physique discussions as a beta-agonist relative of clenbuterol.

It acts on beta-1 and beta-2 receptors, and Wikipedia also describes TAAR1 agonism. In animals it increases muscle protein synthesis and fibre size and reduces fat deposition. Developed by Elanco, it is sold as Paylean for swine, Optaflexx for cattle and Topmax for turkeys. The sources reviewed contain no human trials of deliberate use, and much of the technical literature concerns residue detection.

paras: It is a veterinary product fed to pigs, cattle and turkeys in their last weeks to increase lean gain and feed efficiency. There is no established human use.

Reported effects in people exposed to it include rapid heart rate, tremor, headache, muscle spasm and raised blood pressure. A 2009 EFSA opinion judged the data insufficient to set a safe residue level, and welfare concerns in pigs include hyperactivity and lameness. It is permitted in the US and some other countries and banned in the EU, China and Russia, and residues have triggered anti-doping positives.

angle.text: Ractopamine is a livestock feed additive that promotes lean muscle, and it surfaces in physique discussions as a beta-agonist relative of fat-loss drugs. In animals it raises muscle protein synthesis and reduces fat deposition. No human appearance use is documented; it is mostly known in anti-doping contexts.

lead: Ractopamine hydrochloride is a phenethanolamine beta-adrenergic agonist used as a feed additive in swine, cattle and turkeys to promote lean muscle growth and improve feed efficiency. Elanco Animal Health, formerly part of Eli Lilly, developed it. [1][2][3]

US approval came for swine in 1999, cattle in 2003 and turkeys in 2008. It is banned or restricted in many countries, including the EU, China and Russia, while the US, Canada and Mexico authorize it. [2]
No human clinical studies of deliberate use were identified. Much of the technical literature concerns detecting residues in swine urine and meat. [4][3]
infobox: Permitted in US; banned in EU, China, Russia

paras: Finishing-swine trials in the US and Canada tested ractopamine for performance and carcass characteristics. [5] Wikipedia reports it adds about 3 kg of lean pork per animal and improves feed efficiency by about 10%. [2] Cattle trials have compared it with zilpaterol and clenbuterol. [6][4]

It binds beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors, increasing muscle protein synthesis and shifting nutrient use from fat toward lean tissue. [2][7] Pharmacokinetic and tissue-residue properties of beta-agonists in livestock have been reviewed. [8]

Effects reported in people include tachycardia, tremor, headache, muscle spasm and elevated blood pressure. A 2009 EFSA opinion found the data insufficient to set a safe residue level, especially for children and people with cardiovascular disease. [2]
In swine, reported adverse effects include hyperactivity, trembling and lameness; Temple Grandin has described sore limbs and heat stress in cattle. [2]

Taiwan banned it in 2006. In 2012 the Codex Alimentarius Commission narrowly adopted a 10 ppb maximum residue limit for beef and pork muscle; Russia and China banned it in 2013. [2] The US sets limits of 50 ppb for pork and 30 ppb for beef. [2]

Ractopamine is treated like clenbuterol under the World Anti-Doping Agency's anabolic agents. In 2015 an Egyptian athlete who tested positive received a four-year ineligibility on appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, and a 2017 WADA symposium concluded athletes eating meat with residues at the limit risked positive tests. [2]

No studies found in humans for appearance or performance use. Controlled studies are in swine and cattle. [5][6][4] Environmental and analytical studies address residue detection and veterinary pharmaceuticals in groundwater near livestock facilities. [3][9]
